title: Gaṇeśa Goes Around the World
tease: Two brothers race around the world for a mango. One of them does not leave the room.

source.locus: Rudra Saṃhitā; also Skanda Purāṇa and the Tamil Vināyaka Purāṇam
source.traditionNote: Northern tellings make Kārttikeya the elder brother; Tamil tradition makes Gaṇeśa the elder, which is why Vināyaka is worshipped first. We tell the Tamil shape throughout. The differences are listed below rather than smoothed over.
checkedAgainst: Śiva Purāṇa, Rudra Saṃhitā — Motilal Banarsidass ed.

blocks.text: «Nārada» left one mango in the house, and said that whoever ate it would know everything worth knowing. Then he left, quickly, the way people do when they have handed someone a problem.

There were two boys in that house. «Gaṇeśa», the elder, was round, rode a mouse, and was not fast at all. «Kārttikeya», the younger, was fast — and very proud of being fast. He had a peacock to ride and a spear in his hand.
Both of them wanted the mango.
_A race,_ said «Śiva». _Around the world. First one back gets it._
Kārttikeya was gone before the sentence finished. Gaṇeśa looked at his mouse, and the mouse looked back, and both of them could see how this was going to go.
So «Gaṇeśa» sat down and thought. He knew he could not win by making his mouse faster. He needed to understand what the race was really asking.
Then he got up, walked to his parents, and circled them slowly three times.
And he said: _a world is the thing everything else is inside. Everything I have is inside the two of you. I have been round my world three times. Where is my mango?_
Śiva laughed. «Pārvatī» handed it over.

«Kārttikeya» came back days later, dusty and exhausted, having actually travelled around the world. «Gaṇeśa» was already eating the mango. «Kārttikeya» was furious. In the Tamil telling he went south to «Palani», where he stands with a staff as Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi.
One brother answered the race by travelling around the world. The other answered by asking what _world_ meant. Both moved; only one changed the question.
A sage called «Nārada» came to visit, which in that house was usually a sign that something was about to go wrong.
He had brought one mango, and it was no ordinary fruit. Whoever received it, he said, would gain knowledge.
He handed it to «Śiva» and «Pārvatī» and then left, fairly quickly, the way people do when they have just given someone a problem.
There were two boys in that house.
«Gaṇeśa» was the elder. He was round, rode a mouse, loved his food, and knew perfectly well that speed was not his advantage.
«Kārttikeya» was the younger one. He was fast, rode a peacock, carried a spear, and was very used to winning races.
Both of them wanted the mango.
Their parents had one fruit and two sons who both wanted it, so «Śiva» proposed a race.
_A race,_ said Śiva. _Around the world. First one back gets it._

Kārttikeya was gone before the sentence finished. The peacock went up off the terrace and out over the mountains, and by the time anyone thought to look for him he was a speck, and then he was not even that.
«Kārttikeya» took the challenge literally and did the hard version of it. He flew out on his peacock and travelled around the world, determined to complete the race properly and return first.
Gaṇeśa looked at his mouse.
The mouse looked back at him. Both of them could see how this was going to go.
So he sat down and thought about it.
«Gaṇeśa» did not have the answer immediately. He sat and thought because racing faster was impossible. The only way forward was to understand the word _world_ differently.
And then he got up.
He walked over to where his parents were sitting and circled them slowly. When he returned to his starting place, he had not travelled far, but he was ready with his answer.
Then he did it again. Three times in all.
And he sat down in front of them and said: _a world is the thing everything else is inside. Everything I have is inside the two of you. I have been round my world three times. Where is my mango?_
Śiva laughed. Pārvatī gave him the mango.
«Pārvatī» did not give a long explanation. She handed him the mango because his answer had satisfied the challenge.
When «Kārttikeya» finally returned, dusty and exhausted after actually travelling around the world, his elder brother was already eating the mango.
«Kārttikeya» was furious, and not without reason: he had done exactly what the race seemed to ask.
He argued about the rules. From his point of view, he had completed the harder journey and arrived to find the prize already gone.
In the Tamil tradition, his anger carries him south to «Palani». There he stands as Daṇḍāyudhapāṇi, with a staff and simple cloth, having left the contest and its prize behind.
Both boys answered the challenge. «Kārttikeya» travelled around the world. «Gaṇeśa» stopped to ask what _world_ meant before deciding how to move.

linked.reason: another story where the small, unhurried person turns out to have understood the question

close.question: Gaṇeśa did not go round the world. Do you think he won fairly?
close.seed: Sometimes the clever answer is to check what the question actually meant.

ifTheyAsk.a: It is a fair thing to be annoyed about, and Kārttikeya certainly was. The honest answer is that Gaṇeśa did not break the rule — he read it differently, and his parents accepted the reading. Ask your child which they would have done. Most children under seven side with Gaṇeśa and most over ten side with his brother, which is interesting in itself.

Because he did the thing properly, at enormous cost, and lost to someone who did not leave the room. Younger brothers and sisters know that feeling precisely. The story does not punish him for it — it just tells you where he went, and that he is still there.

ifTheyAsk.q: Did he really have an elephant's head?
ifTheyAsk.a: Yes, in every telling — and how he got it is a separate story, and a harder one, involving his father not recognising him. That one is in the collection for older children. Tonight it is enough that he had it and that nobody in the room found it remarkable.
